title: My descent into America's neo-Nazi movement & how I got out | Christian Picciolini | TEDxMileHigh
summary: Christian Picciolini tells how he became a white supremacist at 14 and led America's first neo-Nazi skinhead gang, then how he left. He shares a counterintuitive approach to countering hate and co-founded Life After Hate.
why_hn: HN points to it as proof that people can leave extremist movements, and as a model of de-radicalization through compassion.

title: How Children Develop Perfect Pitch
summary: Rick Beato discusses a theory of why some children develop perfect pitch, based on early exposure to music. He draws on his experience with his own children.
why_hn: Pointed to in threads on training absolute pitch in children as a practitioner's account.

title: How Do Night Vision Goggles Work?
summary: Veritasium visits the US Navy's Crane facility to test top night vision goggles. It explains how image intensifier tubes and thermal or digital systems work and compares the generations of the technology.
why_hn: Commenters point to it as a clear explanation of the different types of night vision and why analog image intensifiers behave differently from digital ones.

title: dotJS 2012 - Fat - What Is Open Source & Why Do I Feel So Guilty?
summary: A dotJS 2012 conference talk by Fat (of Twitter Bootstrap fame) on what open source really means and why maintainers feel guilty about it. It covers the obligations, expectations and burnout that come with releasing popular open source software, delivered with humor.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a funny and candid first-hand account of the guilt and burnout of a prolific open source developer.

title: What is Bitcoin? (v1)
summary: A two-minute animated introduction to Bitcoin from 2011, explaining it as a peer-to-peer digital currency. It was widely shared in Bitcoin's early days as the standard newcomer explainer.
why_hn: HN commenters sent it to newcomers as a short, simple first explanation of Bitcoin.

title: The Mental Game of Python - Raymond Hettinger [synced version]
summary: Raymond Hettinger's PyBay 2019 talk on the mental strategies he uses when programming in Python, such as chunking, solving a simpler related problem, and repeating tasks manually until patterns emerge. This version is re-synced with the slides.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an entertaining talk on how working memory shapes code and how to reduce cognitive load.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #1027 - Courtney Dauwalter
summary: Joe Rogan interviews ultramarathon runner Courtney Dauwalter shortly after she won the Moab 240 in under 58 hours. She tells stories of enduring extreme fatigue and hallucinations.
why_hn: HN recommends it for her humility and for her stories of persevering through extreme endurance races.

title: Introduction to Investing and Finance - Lesson 1 by Martin Shkreli
summary: The first lesson of Martin Shkreli's introductory investing and finance course, running about two and a half hours. His related tutorials cover reading 10-K filings and building DCF models.
why_hn: HN mentions it with caveats: despite the author's reputation, commenters say it contains good investing and Excel material.

title: Primitive Technology: Forge Blower
summary: A Primitive Technology episode in which the creator builds a bow-drill-driven bark fan to blow air into a fire, using only natural materials. It shows the progression from fanning a fire by hand to a rotary forge blower.
why_hn: HN readers like the channel for showing technology rebuilt from raw materials, and cite it as a vivid example of knowledge building on knowledge.

title: Flanders & Swann - 'First And Second Law'
summary: Flanders and Swann perform 'First and Second Law', a comic song about the laws of thermodynamics, from their 1964 stage show At the Drop of Another Hat. It sets the first and second laws to a deadpan call-and-response routine.
why_hn: HN brings it up whenever thermodynamics or entropy comes up, as the classic comic explanation of the laws.

title: Tested: Magic Leap One Augmented Reality Review!
summary: Adam Savage's Tested spends a week with the Magic Leap One developer kit. They dig into the hardware, display technology, user experience and launch apps.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an in-depth independent review that tempers expectations and adds technical detail beyond Magic Leap's own materials.

title: Noam Chomsky: "Free Markets?"
summary: A 1997 Noam Chomsky talk at Northeastern University about the gap between free-market rhetoric and practice. He argues that business relies heavily on state intervention, and he discusses trade, NAFTA and labour versus capital mobility.
why_hn: Linked repeatedly in threads on monopolies, protectionism, and subsidies, usually as a source for the argument that free markets are an ideology more than a reality.

title: The Fight for the Soul of Seattle | A KOMO News Documentary
summary: A KOMO News documentary about Seattle's homelessness, addiction and street crime. It examines the City Council's policies, shows conditions on the streets and the impact on local businesses, and explores possible solutions.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as an overview of Seattle's deterioration when discussing homelessness and crime in West Coast cities.

title: Richard Feynman on hungry philosophers (or do we see objects or only their light)
summary: A one-minute clip from Richard Feynman's 1979 Auckland lecture in which he answers whether you see an object or only its light. It is a short, playful take on perception and on the use of philosophy.
why_hn: HN uses it to illustrate Feynman's wry view of philosophical questions and perception.

title: Copyright is Brain Damage | Nina Paley | TEDxMaastricht
summary: Nina Paley's TEDxMaastricht talk arguing against copyright and for copyleft and free culture. She argues that restricting ideas harms creativity and that culture belongs to everyone.
why_hn: Brought up in copyright, public domain and AI-training debates as a provocative argument for abolishing copyright.

title: Your Brain at Work
summary: David Rock gives a Google Tech Talk based on his book Your Brain at Work, using neuroscience to explain why focus and productivity are hard at the office. He gives strategies for managing mental energy and distraction.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a general overview of the cognitive science of insight and focus that is useful for developers and knowledge workers.

title: The riddle of experience vs. memory | Daniel Kahneman
summary: In this TED talk, Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman distinguishes the experiencing self from the remembering self, using examples such as vacations and colonoscopies. He explains how the two perceive happiness differently and what that means for economics, policy and self-awareness.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it in threads on happiness and well-being as a clear account of why memory and experience of happiness diverge.

title: Ben Marking's Fake BBC Nuclear Attack Broadcast (Full Resolution, Uncut, Unedited)
summary: A 56-minute fake BBC nuclear attack news broadcast originally made by Ben Marking, re-uploaded in full resolution. It is a fictional breaking-news special depicting nuclear war, and the uploader states it is not real.
why_hn: Commenters bring it up in nuclear-fear and WWIII threads as an unnervingly realistic piece of fictional news coverage.

title: Pink Noise for Ten Hours of Ambient Sound  Blocker  Masker - Burn In - Relaxation
summary: Ten hours of uninterrupted pink noise, intended for relaxation and masking background sound. It is a long ambient audio loop rather than a spoken video.
why_hn: HN users use it as a concentration, sleep and tinnitus aid, preferring steady noise over music.

title: Larnell Lewis Hears "Enter Sandman" For The First Time
summary: Drummer Larnell Lewis hears Metallica's Enter Sandman for the first time on Drumeo and learns to play it by ear, using his musical vocabulary.
why_hn: Cited as an inspiring example of quickly picking up a new piece by ear and of expertise transferring across genres.

title: Optimizing Workspace for Productivity, Focus, & Creativity
summary: A Huberman Lab episode on setting up a workspace for productivity, focus and creativity, covering light, posture, movement and sound. It touches on ideas like ceiling height and the effect of screens on the brain.
why_hn: Pointed to when people ask for science-based ways to boost concentration or arrange a home office.

title: Who's faster around London: a taxi driver or a GPS?
summary: Tom Scott races a London black-cab driver who has memorized The Knowledge against a phone GPS across the city, comparing local expertise to navigation software.
why_hn: HN people link it in discussions of taxi drivers' spatial memory and how cabbies handle roadworks and traffic.

title: AI Ethics, Impossibility Theorems and Tradeoffs - Chris Stucchio | Crunch 2018
summary: Chris Stucchio presents the ethical principles behind algorithmic decision making and shows with examples from lending, criminology and education that they cannot all be satisfied at once. The talk frames AI fairness as a set of quantitative tradeoffs.
why_hn: HN cites it in algorithmic-bias threads for the impossibility result that an algorithm cannot be procedurally fair, group fair and maximally useful at once.

title: The Future Of Reasoning
summary: Vsauce explores how human reasoning works, drawing on the social theory of reason and the extended mind thesis, made in partnership with Bill Gates around climate change.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it for the social theory that reasoning evolved as a collaborative activity, and one lists it as a favorite video.

title: Sloane's Gap - Numberphile
summary: A Numberphile video with Dr James Grime on Sloane's Gap, the observation that integers in the OEIS are not evenly represented and some numbers are underrepresented. It explains the clusters of 'interesting' numbers.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a concise, quick explanation of the OEIS pattern when threads touch the integer sequence encyclopedia.

title: Moon Landings Faked? Filmmaker Says Not!
summary: A filmmaker explains why the Apollo moon landing footage could not have been faked in a studio, based on the video and film technology of the late 1960s. He walks through the limits of cameras, frame rates and effects of the era.
why_hn: HN points to it as a concise, technically grounded rebuttal to moon-hoax claims.

title: Cities Without People
summary: Jacob Geller's video essay on empty cities and what they say about our relationship to places, using games, literature and aerial imagery. It touches on works such as Invisible Cities.
why_hn: HN points to Geller's essays as accessible companions to literary works and as a good summary of a story.

title: New vs Old Room Fire Final UL
summary: A short NIST-based demonstration places a room furnished with old natural-material furniture beside one with modern synthetic furnishings and burns both. The modern room reaches full flashover in a few minutes while the legacy room is only starting to spread.
why_hn: HN uses it as vivid proof that modern fires develop much faster, which is the argument for working smoke detectors and early escape.

title: DEFCON 19: Bit-squatting: DNS Hijacking Without Exploitation (w speaker)
summary: Artem Dinaburg's DEF CON 19 talk on bit-squatting, where flipped bits in DRAM cause devices to contact domains that differ by one bit from legitimate ones. He shows how registering such domains can hijack traffic without exploiting any software bug.
why_hn: HN cites it in ECC memory debates and bit-flip discussions as concrete evidence that memory errors have real security consequences.

title: GopherCon 2015: Go GC: Solving the Latency Problem - Rick Hudson
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Rick Hudson's GopherCon 2015 talk on Go 1.5's new low-latency concurrent garbage collector. It covers the motivation, performance numbers, technical challenges and why the approach fits Go.
why_hn: Pointed to as the authoritative source on Go's GC pause improvements, and later revisited when GC latency claims were challenged.

title: Aldous Huxley interviewed by Mike Wallace : 1958 (Full)
summary: Mike Wallace interviews Aldous Huxley in 1958 about the warnings in Brave New World, including mass persuasion, overpopulation and voluntary totalitarianism.
why_hn: Recommended as more thought-provoking than the usual pill-popping take on Huxley.

title: The Secret Reason We Eat Meat - Dr. Melanie Joy
summary: Social psychologist Melanie Joy introduces the concept of carnism, the belief system that conditions people to eat some animals but not others.
why_hn: HN offers it as a short, light introduction to carnism and the language bias around eating animals.

title: We all move at the Speed of Light
summary: ScienceClic explains why nothing can go faster than light by treating motion through space and time together, so everything moves at the speed of light through spacetime. It uses animated visuals to cover relativity basics in 12 minutes.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a helpful way to conceptualize why light speed is a limit.

title: Chris Seaton @ VMSS16: JRuby+Truffle: Why it’s Important to Optimise the Tricky Parts
summary: Chris Seaton talks about JRuby+Truffle, explaining how the Truffle and Graal combination optimises the tricky parts of Ruby and why it outperforms other Ruby implementations.
why_hn: HN recommends it for specifics on how Truffle and Graal achieve strong dynamic-language performance.

title: Node.js Is Bad Ass Rock Star Tech
summary: A short satirical sketch in which a Q&A about web servers turns into a profane rant about threads, blocking and non-blocking I/O. It lampoons the hype around Node.js and async programming.
why_hn: HN mostly drops it as a joke in async, Node and concurrency threads, and some call it hysterically funny.

title: David Kriesel: Lies, damned lies and scans
channel: Free and Open Source Software Conference (FrOSCon) e.V.
summary: David Kriesel's FrOSCon talk on how Xerox scancopiers, due to JBIG2 compression, silently replaced digits in scanned documents. He walks through how he discovered the bug and why it is so dangerous.
why_hn: The standard reference whenever HN discusses the Xerox scanner bug or AI and compression that fabricates content.

title: Everything Is A Remix (Full Film)
summary: Kirby Ferguson's film argues that creativity is built from copying, transforming and combining existing works, examining music, film and technology. It makes the case that everything is a remix.
why_hn: HN brings it up in discussions of originality, invention, copying and attribution, including AI art.

title: What Happened Before History? Human Origins
summary: Kurzgesagt's animated overview of human origins and the vast prehistory before recorded history. It covers how modern humans emerged and spread.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a compact, well-sourced intro to human evolution that even led one viewer to read Sapiens.

title: Planes clouds and vortices
summary: A short compilation of aircraft flying through clouds and moist air, showing the spiraling vortices that wings leave behind. The footage shows wingtip vortices and the way planes disturb cloud layers.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as a visual illustration of wingtip vortices and wake turbulence when discussing lift and aircraft wakes.

title: Swami Sarvapriyananda at IITK - "Who Am I?" according to Mandukya Upanishad-Part 1
summary: A lecture by Swami Sarvapriyananda at IIT Kanpur on the Mandukya Upanishad and the question 'Who am I?'. It explains the four states of consciousness in Advaita Vedanta.
why_hn: Recommended in threads about consciousness and reality as a clear exposition of the Vedantic view of waking, dreaming and deep sleep.

title: 7 Habits For Effective Text Editing 2.0
summary: Vim author Bram Moolenaar's 2007 Google Tech Talk on habits for efficient text editing: find inefficiencies in your own editing, then learn the Vim commands that fix them.
why_hn: Recommended as practical advice straight from Vim's author, and shared in memory of Bram after his death.

title: Hovering a Helicopter is Hilariously Hard - Smarter Every Day 145
summary: Smarter Every Day host Destin Sandlin tries to hover a helicopter and finds it very hard. The video shows how the constant coordinated corrections across several control axes feel at first and how learning makes them automatic.
why_hn: HN uses it as a vivid example of tacit knowledge and skill acquisition, where the brain eventually abstracts away the complexity.

title: The Fall of Minecraft's 2b2t
summary: FitMC tells how the Nocom exploit let griefers track players across Minecraft's oldest anarchy server, 2b2t, and the fallout that followed.
why_hn: Cited as the original, accurate account of the Nocom exploit, a story of years of player tracking and impressive technical work.

title: The most important lesson from 83,000 brain scans | Daniel Amen | TEDxOrangeCoast
summary: Psychiatrist Daniel Amen discusses lessons from 83,000 brain scans, arguing that brain activity patterns relate to psychological symptoms and that you can improve your brain.
why_hn: HN cites it in depression and brain health threads for its message that the brain can be improved, and that brain injury is common and overlooked.

title: Is Your Red The Same as My Red?
summary: Vsauce explores qualia and whether different people experience colors the same way. It draws on color blindness, Mary's room, the explanatory gap and subjective experience.
why_hn: HN points people to it as an accessible explanation of what qualia are.

title: Lisp at the Frontier of Computation, by Robert Smith at Rigetti Computing
summary: Robert Smith of Rigetti Computing talks at a Bay Area Lisp and Scheme meetup about using Common Lisp for quantum computing. He covers the technical, sociological and psychological sides of working across disciplines.
why_hn: Recommended as a real-world case of Lisp in a cutting-edge industry, applied to quantum hardware.

why_hn: Cited in threads about recommendation algorithms and clickbait as a creator's inside view of why optimizing for click-through rate shapes content.

title: Liquid Democracy In Simple Terms
summary: A five-minute animated explainer of liquid democracy, in which voters can delegate their vote to trusted people. It starts from the origins of democracy and contrasts direct and representative models.
why_hn: HN users share it as a brief, good introduction whenever liquid or delegative democracy comes up.

title: The illusion of consciousness | Dan Dennett
summary: Philosopher Dan Dennett argues in a TED talk that we do not understand our own consciousness and that our brains often fool us. He uses perceptual examples, including a painting that invites the viewer to fill in detail.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short route to Dennett's view of consciousness as a bag of tricks, often in AI and cognition threads.

title: Jordan Peterson - IQ and The Job Market
summary: A clip of Jordan Peterson arguing that IQ is a strong predictor of job market success and that more complex jobs demand higher cognitive ability. He discusses what this means for people left behind.
why_hn: HN cites it in threads on jobs, automation and hiring when arguing about IQ and employability.

title: The Material Science of Metal 3D Printing
summary: Real Engineering explains the materials science behind metal 3D printing, including crystal structure, laser sintering, and why printed parts develop fatigue cracks. It shows how process imperfections limit the strength of printed metal.
why_hn: Commenters point to it whenever 3D-printed metal parts come up, as a clear explanation of why they have poor fatigue life and material defects.

title: The Stuff of Thought | Steven Pinker | Talks at Google
summary: Steven Pinker presents his book The Stuff of Thought at Google in 2007. He covers language as a window into human nature, including taboo words, swearing and the psychology and game theory of indirect speech like bribery.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it for Pinker's analysis of profanity and of why talking about taboo words differs from using them.

title: How AI Could Save (Not Destroy) Education | Sal Khan | TED
summary: Sal Khan of Khan Academy gives a TED talk on how AI could transform education, with a personal tutor for every student and a teaching assistant for every teacher. He demos Khanmigo, including features where the AI reasons before responding.
why_hn: Cited in AI-and-education threads as the optimistic case and demo for AI tutoring, and as a source on Khan Academy's LLM approach.

title: Cyclists' hearts: can you be so fit that you die?

title: John Schulman - Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: Progress and Challenges

title: Illustrating Crafting Interpreters

title: Positive Affirmations for Site Reliability Engineers
summary: A KRAZAM comedy sketch in which a character recites reassuring affirmations to site reliability engineers, satirizing on-call and outage culture.
why_hn: Shared as comic relief that hits close to home for people who work with infrastructure at scale.

title: Babel Fish - The Oddest Thing In The Universe - The Hitchhiker's Guide To The Galaxy - BBC
summary: The BBC TV version of the Babel Fish passage from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, with Ford and Arthur aboard a Vogon ship, narrated over the show's hand-drawn animated Guide entry.
why_hn: HN points to it for the memorable hand-animated computer graphics, which still hold up, and as the TV rendition of a famous passage.

title: PHILOSOPHY - Albert Camus
summary: A School of Life animated overview of Albert Camus, covering his existentialism and absurdism and his answer to the question of meaninglessness.
why_hn: Offered as an accessible introduction to Camus and absurdism.

title: Jaron Lanier interview on how social media ruins your life

why_hn: Offered as a concise summary of the economics and manipulation behind social media addiction in Facebook-related threads.

title: Do you know this guy? | Internet Explorer
summary: A two-minute Microsoft ad for Internet Explorer 10 in which a karaoke-style song addresses people who hate the browser. It is part of the "browser you loved to hate" campaign.
why_hn: Cited in threads about IE's reputation as an example of Microsoft's self-aware, funny advertising.

title: Your Brain Hallucinates Your Conscious Reality | Anil Seth | TED
summary: Neuroscientist Anil Seth argues in this TED talk that perception is a controlled hallucination: the brain constantly predicts the world and our shared agreement is what we call reality. He also touches on the construction of the self.

title: Unconscious Bias @ Work | Google Ventures
summary: A Google Ventures talk on how unconscious biases shape product decisions, hiring and workplace interactions. It draws on research, including work by Google scientists, on how to counter them.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an interesting look at the psychology research behind bias in hiring and performance reviews.

title: Why Teleportation Would Kill You
summary: CGP Grey asks whether Star Trek-style teleportation would kill you and recreate a copy, working through the philosophy of identity and the Ship of Theseus. It is a short animated explainer.
why_hn: Pointed to in threads about mind uploading and teleportation as a good, accessible look at personal identity.

summary: ContraPoints' long-form video response to Jordan Peterson, critiquing his ideas including his use of the term postmodern neo-Marxism. It is delivered in her theatrical essay style.
why_hn: HN mostly cites it as the go-to critique of Peterson when his positions or advice come up.

title: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking | Daniel Dennett | Talks at Google
summary: Philosopher Daniel Dennett visits Google to discuss his book Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking, describing thought experiments and thinking tools across psychology, biology, computer science and physics.
why_hn: Pointed to as an accessible introduction to intuition pumps as thinking tools, and shared in remembrance after Dennett's death.

title: Office Space - If I had a million dollars
summary: A 54-second clip from the film Office Space in which two coworkers talk about what they would do with a million dollars. The answers contrast blue-collar and white-collar attitudes toward work.
why_hn: Mostly a joke reference in threads about layoffs, idleness and wealth, with one commenter sincerely recommending the clip for its contrast of work attitudes.

title: Building Brains to Understand the World's Data
summary: Jeff Hawkins presents his view that the neocortex works on principles different from traditional computers. He describes sparse distributed representations and how they are learned, then shows how Numenta applies them to predict from high-velocity data streams.
why_hn: Recommended as Hawkins' own accessible statement of his brain-inspired theory of intelligence and its software implementation.

title: Noam Chomsky - The Crimes of U.S. Presidents
summary: A short clip, from 2003, of Noam Chomsky going through crimes of post-WW2 US presidents. He argues that they would be indictable under the Nuremberg principles.
why_hn: HN links it as the source for the claim that every post-war president would be indictable under Nuremberg standards.

title: Former KGB Agent Yuri Bezmenov Explains How to Brainwash a Nation (Full Length)
summary: A long interview with former KGB agent Yuri Bezmenov describing what he calls ideological subversion, a process of demoralizing a nation. He claims it works by influencing academia and media over years.
why_hn: HN commenters mostly cite it in political threads as a theory of subversion, and several mentions are repeated drive-by posts.

title: CANDO: A Compiled Programming Language for Computer-Aided Nanomaterial Design and Optimization
summary: Christian Schafmeister presents CANDO at the 2016 European Lisp Symposium. It is a compiled Lisp-based language for designing macromolecules and nanoscale materials, built on the Clasp implementation of Common Lisp.
why_hn: Recommended as one of the best talks of the symposium for the unusual scope of applying Lisp to molecular design.

title: Yann Lecun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #416
summary: Lex Fridman's long podcast interview with Yann LeCun on Meta AI, open source, the limits of LLMs, AGI and the future of AI.
why_hn: Cited for LeCun's views on LLM limits and alternative approaches to intelligence.

title: Revealed: ExxonMobil’s lobbying war on climate change legislation
summary: Channel 4 News reports on undercover Greenpeace footage of an ExxonMobil lobbyist describing efforts to weaken climate legislation. Exxon disputes the claims.
why_hn: Cited as a source on oil industry lobbying and disinformation in climate policy threads.

title: Air Conditioning isn't free... but we're close.
summary: Tech Ingredients shows how to build a liquid panel with a specialty paint that, placed outside, cools below ambient air temperature. It demonstrates radiative sky cooling.
why_hn: HN points to it in threads on radiative cooling as a hands-on explanation of passive daytime cooling.

title: Milton Friedman - I, Pencil
summary: A two-minute clip in which Milton Friedman uses a humble pencil to show how thousands of strangers across many countries cooperate, without central direction, to make a simple product. It is a short visual version of the 'I, Pencil' essay's argument about free markets and dispersed knowledge.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as the quick, shareable illustration of hidden supply-chain complexity and decentralized knowledge, and bring it up in threads on AI, manufacturing and specialization.

title: How dangerous are magnetic items near an MRI magnet?
summary: A three-minute demonstration with a decommissioned 4 tesla MRI magnet showing how magnetic objects are pulled in and oscillate along the bore. It illustrates the safety hazards of ferromagnetic items near MRI scanners.
why_hn: Linked in threads on magnets and implants as a vivid demonstration of how violent MRI magnet forces are.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #1006 - Jordan Peterson & Bret Weinstein
summary: A long Joe Rogan Experience podcast episode with psychologist Jordan Peterson and biologist Bret Weinstein, recorded during the controversy at Evergreen State College. They discuss campus politics, polarization, ideology and related social topics.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a wide-ranging conversation on political polarization and free discussion, and one commenter points to a segment on wealth distribution following a square-root law.

title: Alexander Nix: From Mad Men to Math Men | OMR Festival 2017 - Hamburg, Germany | #OMR17
summary: Cambridge Analytica CEO Alexander Nix keynotes the OMR 2017 marketing festival on big data and personality-based targeting in political campaigns. It was given before the company's scandal broke.
why_hn: HN cites it, often critically, as Nix openly describing data-driven manipulation and targeting methods.

title: Space Shades: Humanity's Last Hope | Answers With Joe
summary: Joe Scott takes a serious look at space sunshades as a climate fix, asking how big they would need to be, what they would cost and whether they would work. He draws on Roger Angel's paper and launch options.
why_hn: Linked as a worked look at the maths and assumptions of orbital sunshades, which concludes they are impractical.

title: Charles Babbage and Difference Enginge No. 2 | Doron Swade | Talks at Google
summary: Historian Doron Swade tells the story of Charles Babbage's quest to build the Difference Engine and the construction of Difference Engine No. 2 at the Science Museum. The talk covers Babbage's motivation, his machines and Ada Lovelace's insight into the Analytical Engine.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as a source on Babbage's machines, especially for the section around minute 36 on Ada Lovelace's insight beyond numeric computation.

title: Live ClojureScript Game Editor
summary: A five-minute demo of a live ClojureScript game editor by Chris Granger. It is based on Bret Victor's demo from the Inventing on Principle talk, with code changes reflected instantly in the running game.
why_hn: Cited as an early example of live coding applied beyond debugging, and as precursor to Light Table.

title: Where Does Bad Code Come From?
summary: Casey Muratori's invited lecture on where bad code comes from, rebroadcast from a Twitch stream. He critiques conventional wisdom such as SOLID and Clean Code and argues about how those habits lead to slow, poorly structured software.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a sharp critique of SOLID, Clean Code and 'non-pessimized' programming, and as context for why software is getting worse.

title: TRON Smart House
summary: A short video of the first TRON Smart House, built in 1989 as a demonstration of ubiquitous and ambient computing in the home. It comes from the uID Center, which promoted the TRON architecture.
why_hn: HN cites it as the concrete demo behind discussions of Japan's TRON project and early smart-home ideas.

title: Joe Rogan on Why he changed his stance on the Moon landing conspiracy
summary: A clip from Joe Rogan Experience #928 in which Rogan, with Arian Foster, explains why he abandoned his belief in Moon landing conspiracy theories. He describes how doctored training photos fueled doubt before he learned more of the physics.
why_hn: Cited as an example of someone publicly changing their mind on the Moon landing hoax and of why skeptics had rational-seeming doubts.

title: Servo: Building a Parallel Browser
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Jack Moffitt presents Servo, an experimental browser engine written in Rust and designed to be parallel at every level, using multiple cores, the GPU, fork-join concurrency and SIMD. The talk covers motivations, architecture and plans for the project.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a detailed source on Servo's design and performance, including plans to move Servo code into Gecko.

title: They're Made Out of Meat
summary: A short film adaptation of Terry Bisson's story 'They're Made Out of Meat', in which alien explorers discuss with disbelief that humans are sentient beings made of meat. It won a grand prize at the 2006 SIFF short film festival.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a well-made version of the story and quote it jokingly whenever discussions touch on biology versus machine intelligence.

title: Your elusive creative genius | Elizabeth Gilbert
summary: Elizabeth Gilbert, author of Eat, Pray, Love, reflects on the pressure placed on artists to be geniuses. She proposes the older idea that creative people have a genius that visits them rather than being one.
why_hn: HN people link it in threads about creativity, late bloomers and creative burnout as a humble, relatable take on where inspiration comes from.

title: "Weird Al" Yankovic - Word Crimes (Official 4K Video)
summary: Weird Al Yankovic's 2014 parody of 'Blurred Lines' that scolds common grammar and usage errors, with a kinetic typography video. It is a catchy music video about language mistakes.
why_hn: HN mostly drops it jokingly in threads about grammar, apostrophes and language, and occasionally discusses the animated video's making.

title: Event Sourcing • Greg Young • GOTO 2014
summary: Greg Young, who coined CQRS, gives an in-depth GOTO 2014 talk on what event sourcing is, when it is valuable and when it is not, along with its trade-offs and common misconceptions.
why_hn: HN commenters list it among the best introductions to event sourcing and use it to illustrate storing read-only events instead of mutating state.

title: Adam Curtis - Oh Dearism
summary: A short Adam Curtis clip on what he calls oh dearism, the habit of news reporting that presents events as a stream of sad, inexplicable happenings. He argues this leaves viewers passive and unable to imagine action.
why_hn: Shared as a compact critique of how news framing breeds passivity and despair.

title: Can we build AI without losing control over it? | Sam Harris
summary: Sam Harris argues in a TED talk that we will build superhuman AI and have not grappled with the risk of creating something that may treat us the way we treat ants. He makes a logical case for taking AI risk seriously.
why_hn: HN cites it in AI risk debates, sometimes as an argument that has aged well and sometimes as an example of alarmist framing.

title: Pointing and Calling Japanese Safety Standard at Railway Companies & Toyota (HD)
summary: A short documentary clip of Japanese railway workers and Toyota staff using pointing-and-calling, a safety practice of physically pointing at and naming things while working. It includes examples from several railway companies.
why_hn: HN finds it fascinating and suggests the technique for keeping operators like test drivers attentive.

title: The Light It Up Contest -- geohot
summary: A one-minute rap by George Hotz (geohot) aimed at Sony, made as an entry for a contest while Sony was suing him over the PS3 jailbreak. It is a humorous diss track delivered from the middle of the lawsuit.
why_hn: HN mostly brings it up as a funny, cocky artifact of the Hotz-versus-Sony fight, sometimes with a skeptical eye on how seriously he took the lawsuit.

title: Interview with FFMPEG enthusiast
summary: Kai Lentit's comedy sketch parodying an interview with an FFmpeg enthusiast. It pokes fun at the open source command-line tool experience and video conversion woes.
why_hn: Shared as obligatory humor in FFmpeg and video tooling threads, praised as a funny take on the open source user experience.

title: The Daily Show - Gun Control Whoop-de-doo (ft. John Oliver)
summary: A Daily Show segment in which John Oliver examines the argument that gun control does not work, using Australia's experience after the Senate rejected the Manchin-Toomey amendment. It is a comedic, man-on-the-street style piece.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a humorous but pointed look at gun control and at learning from other countries' policies.

title: Corporate Music - How to Compose with no Soul
summary: Composer Tantacrul explores how corporatism produces soulless background music, and how some companies use such music in propaganda-style campaigns. He composes several corporate styles to show their tropes, with some music theory along the way.
why_hn: HN uses it as a go-to critique of bland corporate music and as a punchline whenever a slick corporate video appears.

title: "Silicon Valley Story"  — a Very Short Romantic Comedy by Ted Nelson
summary: A short romantic comedy by Ted Nelson about the 'microcircuitry of love', with Doug Engelbart as his father and Stewart Brand as the villainous CEO.
why_hn: Mentioned in Nelson and Engelbart threads as a curiosity with amusing cameos by computing pioneers.

title: Liam – An Innovation Story
summary: A short Apple promotional video about Liam, a robot that disassembles old iPhones so their materials can be recovered. It frames the robot as part of Apple's product life cycle and recycling story.
why_hn: Cited in repair and recycling threads as Apple's showcase of its iPhone disassembly robot, and sometimes mocked as marketing for what is really shredding.

title: Eliezer Yudkowsky: Dangers of AI and the End of Human Civilization | Lex Fridman Podcast #368
summary: A three-hour Lex Fridman podcast conversation with AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky about the dangers of superintelligent AI and his argument that it could end human civilization. It covers AI alignment, why he thinks LLM capabilities are poorly understood, and the case for extreme caution.
why_hn: Mostly cited as the canonical statement of AI doomer views, with some recommending it and many criticizing it as irresponsible or wrong.

title: Hal fixing a light bulb (from Malcolm in the Middle S03E06 - Health Scare)
summary: A short scene from Malcolm in the Middle in which Hal tries to fix a light bulb and is pulled into a growing chain of side repairs.
why_hn: The standard illustration of yak shaving, dependency hell and getting derailed, also likened to adult ADHD.

title: The IGF-1 Trade-Off: Performance vs. Longevity
summary: A short FoundMyFitness explainer on the trade-off between growth hormone/IGF-1 and longevity. Higher IGF-1 helps muscle and cognition, while lower levels are linked to longer lifespan and stress resistance.
why_hn: Linked in discussions of diet, aging and cancer as a quick summary of how IGF-1 and mTOR growth signaling cut against longevity.

title: Black Hat 2013 - Exploiting Network Surveillance Cameras Like a Hollywood Hacker
summary: Craig Heffner's Black Hat 2013 talk on exploiting network surveillance cameras, covering how insecure their firmware is. It shows how easily such devices can be compromised.
why_hn: HN cites it as a fun and damning illustration of how poor security is in IP cameras, even expensive ones.

title: Empire Files: How Palestine Became Colonized
summary: An Empire Files episode giving a timeline of Zionist settlement, the Nakba and Israel's expansion over Palestinian land, presented from a critical, anti-colonial viewpoint. It previews Abby Martin's reporting in Palestine.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as a history of Palestine's colonization, though others dismiss it as propaganda.

title: Guilty until proven innocent.
summary: A compilation of police interrogations of innocent suspects who behave in very different ways yet are treated as guilty. It illustrates how interrogation tactics and detectives' assumptions can distort the truth.
why_hn: HN commenters use it to show that behavior in interrogations is not a reliable sign of guilt and that police lie to innocent people.

title: 14. Limbic System
summary: Robert Sapolsky's Stanford lecture on the limbic system as the emotional part of the nervous system, covering its role in decision making, links to the cortex and the functions of its subparts.
why_hn: HN cites it as a real academic source to back up or correct claims about emotion, anger and anxiety in the brain.

title: Chris Crawford Dragon Speech "I Had a Dream"
summary: Chris Crawford's 'Dragon Speech' from the first Game Developers Conference, in which he reflects on his dream for game design as an art form. This is a cleaned-up version of the old recording.
why_hn: HN people mention it as a notable historical talk from the early game industry, though some see it as showing his eccentricity.

title: Tom Lehrer - National Brotherhood Week - with intro
summary: Tom Lehrer performs his satirical song "National Brotherhood Week" with a spoken intro. The song mocks superficial displays of tolerance while prejudices between groups carry on.
why_hn: Mostly quoted or linked as a witty example of Lehrer's satire, often as a joke in unrelated threads.

title: Why is light slower in glass? - Sixty Symbols
summary: Professor Mike Merrifield of Nottingham explains in a mostly uncut conversation why light travels slower in glass. He treats light as a wave and describes how the material's electrons produce secondary waves that combine to slow it.
why_hn: HN cites it whenever the popular absorb-and-re-emit explanation comes up, as a source for the wave-interference account.

title: Does the language you speak change how you think?
summary: Tom Scott, with linguists Gretchen McCulloch and Molly Ruhl, examines whether the language you speak changes how you think. The short answer is mostly no, with caveats about the weak version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis.
why_hn: Linked as a concise, accessible rebuttal whenever linguistic relativity comes up in a thread.

title: Tesla Bot Update | Sort & Stretch
summary: A short Tesla clip showing the Optimus humanoid robot sorting objects autonomously and doing yoga-style stretches. Tesla says its neural network is trained end to end, from video in to controls out.
why_hn: Linked as a data point on the state of humanoid robot manipulation in 2023.

title: Michael Drives Into A Lake  - The Office US
summary: A short scene from The Office US in which Michael Scott blindly follows his GPS and drives into a lake. The tagline is never trust technology.
why_hn: HN people link it as a joke about blindly trusting navigation or automated systems.

title: Computational Design of Mechanical Characters
summary: A Disney Research SIGGRAPH 2013 demo of an interactive system that lets non-experts design animated mechanical characters. The user sketches motion curves and the system generates optimized mechanisms and gear trains for 3D printing.
why_hn: HN cites it as an example of computational mechanism design, especially in threads on gears, linkages and animatronics.

title: Macintosh Factory
summary: A video tour of Apple's highly automated Macintosh factory in Fremont, California, where the Mac SE and Macintosh II were built.
why_hn: Used as the visual reference for Apple's earlier US manufacturing and automation, often as an example of factory automation lessons.
